articles.title: Goodbye CPAP? New sleep apnea pill cuts breathing events by 44%
articles.summary: A once-nightly pill cut breathing interruptions by about 44% in a major phase 3 sleep apnea trial, while improving oxygen levels and disease severity. By strengthening the muscles that keep the airway open during sleep, AD109 could offer a new option for people unable to tolerate CPAP.
articles.content:
A once-nightly oral medication significantly improved obstructive sleep apnea in a large phase 3 clinical trial presented at the 2026 ATS International Conference. The drug, known as AD109, is designed to treat OSA by targeting the neuromuscular problems that contribute to airway collapse during sleep.

The study, "Aroxybutynin and Atomoxetine (AD109) for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Randomized Phase 3 Trial," was published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine.

In the SynAIRgy trial, people who received AD109 experienced fewer interruptions in breathing, less oxygen deprivation, and better overall blood oxygen levels while they slept. More than 40 percent improved enough to move into a less severe OSA category, while 18 percent achieved complete disease control.

"These results provide encouraging evidence that targeting neuromuscular dysfunction can translate into meaningful clinical outcomes, aligning with our evolving understanding of the disease biology," said first author Patrick John Strollo, MD, a sleep medicine physician at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center.

A Potential Alternative for People Who Cannot Use CPAP

Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) remains the gold standard treatment for OSA, but many people have difficulty tolerating it. Dr. Strollo said AD109 could provide another option for patients who are unable or unwilling to use CPAP.

"In many other chronic diseases, such as cardiovascular disease, asthma, or type 2 diabetes, it would be unthinkable for the majority of diagnosed patients to remain untreated or undertreated. Yet that remains the reality in OSA," he said. "An oral pill that targets the underlying neuromuscular drivers of airway collapse during sleep could help address this gap and broaden the range of effective options for patients who remain untreated today."

AD109 combines two drugs, aroxybutynin and atomoxetine. Together, they are intended to support the muscles of the throat so the airway is less likely to sag or collapse during sleep.

Breathing Interruptions Fell by About 44 Percent

Researchers conducted the six-month trial at 69 sites in the U.S. and Canada. A total of 646 adults with mild to severe OSA participated, all of whom had either refused CPAP or were unable to tolerate it.

Among patients who took AD109, the apnea-hypoxia index, which measures the number of breathing interruptions per hour, fell by about 44 percent. By comparison, the reduction was 18 percent among participants who received a placebo.

Other measures of nighttime oxygen problems also improved. These included the oxygen desaturation index (the number of times during the night that blood oxygen drops) and hypoxic burden (oxygen deficiency).

The benefits were seen across a wide variety of patients, including people with different levels of disease severity and different body types.

Side Effects and Treatment Discontinuation

AD109 also showed an acceptable safety profile, with side effects that researchers described as mild and expected. The most frequently reported side effects were dry mouth, nausea, insomnia, and difficulty urinating.

About 21 percent of patients stopped taking the treatment because of side effects.

Dr. Strollo said the clinical findings will be published alongside a companion mechanistic review by ATS in the American Journal of Respiratory Cell and Molecular Biology.

"Together, these peer-reviewed articles connect late-stage clinical outcomes with the biological mechanisms that drive the disease, targeted by the mechanism of action of AD109, providing a more complete and integrated view of OSA and strengthening confidence in the approach," he said.

FDA Review Could Come Next

AD109 has received Fast Track designation from the FDA for the treatment of OSA, reflecting the need for effective and well-tolerated drug therapies for the condition.

Apnimed has submitted its New Drug Application (NDA) for AD109 to the FDA. Based on feedback from the agency, the company expects a potential PDUFA target action date in 1Q 2027, provided the FDA accepts the NDA for review.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant medical breakthrough in treating obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) with a new oral medication (AD109) that substantially reduces breathing interruptions and improves oxygen levels. This offers a promising alternative to CPAP, the current standard treatment, for many patients who cannot tolerate it. The large phase 3 clinical trial with 646 participants and FDA Fast Track designation highlight the broad significance and potential real-world impact on millions affected by OSA.

articles.title: Mindfulness may lower blood pressure in just 8 weeks
articles.summary: Mindfulness, gratitude, and optimism training may improve blood pressure, inflammation, and other heart-health measures within just eight to 12 weeks. The strongest programs paired daily practice with regular reinforcement, suggesting that improving psychological well-being could become another tool for protecting cardiovascular health.
articles.content:
Simple practices such as mindfulness, gratitude journaling, and optimism training may improve several markers of cardiovascular health within a matter of weeks. A recent study found that these positive psychology interventions were consistently associated with improvements in blood pressure, inflammation, and other heart disease risk factors. Because some of the benefits appeared to be connected with healthier behaviors, including better eating habits and increased physical activity, the researchers said continued reinforcement may be necessary to maintain progress over time.

Rosalba (Rose) Hernandez, a professor of social work at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, led the research team. The group reviewed results from 18 randomized controlled trials that tested positive psychology and mindfulness interventions designed to improve mental or physical health.

How the Heart Health Programs Worked

The programs varied widely in how they were delivered. Some relied on structured phone sessions, journaling paired with brief check-ins, or digital tools such as apps and text messages. Others involved interactive in-person group meetings or hybrid approaches that combined face-to-face activities with online tools and virtual sessions.

Most programs included weekly sessions along with activities participants completed at home to reinforce what they had learned. The majority lasted between six and 12 weeks.

The studies generally enrolled groups of 50-200 adults who already had elevated cardiovascular risk, including uncontrolled hypertension, heart failure, or other health conditions. Participants were usually in their late 50s to mid-60s. Among studies that reported gender, women made up 35-55% of the participants.

"In hypertension and postacute coronary syndrome cohorts, mindfulness-based programs delivered over an eight-week period reduced systolic blood pressure and lowered inflammatory markers such as high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and fibrinogen," said Hernandez, who is a Fellow of the American Heart Association. "A 12-week spirituality-based digital intervention achieved one of the largest reductions -- reducing systolic blood pressure measured with a standard cuff by 7.6 points, and central systolic pressure -- which is measured in the aorta as it leaves the heart -- by 4.1 points."

Finding the Right "Dose" of Positivity

Previous research on positive psychology often did not clearly establish how frequently people needed to practice these techniques, or for how long, to gain health benefits, Hernandez said. Her team wanted to determine what level of participation was most consistently associated with improvements in cardiovascular health.

The review showed that programs with more frequent participant contact tended to produce the most reliable physiological benefits. Hernandez said this finding highlights the potential value of incorporating positive psychology strategies into long-term cardiovascular treatment and prevention.

The strongest behavioral changes came from an eight-week WhatsApp-based program that paired weekly sessions with daily microtasks. Participants were encouraged to become more physically active, improve their diets, and take their medications as prescribed.

Another program that incorporated motivational interviewing increased cardiac patients' activity by 1,800 steps per day while also improving medication adherence. By comparison, the mindfulness programs improved physical activity and diet, but did not produce the same medication adherence benefit, according to the study.

"The therapeutic dose that was most consistently linked with improvements in blood pressure, inflammation and endothelial function was daily practice reinforced by weekly sessions over eight to 12-week periods," Hernandez said. "Therapeutic dosing typically involved high-frequency dosing over this time period to obtain short-term physiologic benefits, while ongoing less-intensive contact may be needed to sustain behavioral change."

Mental Health as Part of Heart Care

The study was published in the journal Cardiology Clinics. Co-authors included University of South Florida social work professor Soonhyung Kwon; Alyssa M. Vela, a professor of surgery and of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine; and Katharine S. Edwards, a professor of cardiovascular medicine and of psychiatry and behavioral medicine at Stanford Medicine.

"The findings of this study further point to the importance of attending to mental and behavioral health for cardiovascular disease prevention and cardiovascular health optimization," Vela said. "This speaks to the need for routine screening and integration of cardiac behavioral medicine to allow for access to important interventions."

The findings contribute to a growing body of evidence connecting psychological well-being with cardiovascular protection. Traits and experiences such as optimism, positive affect, and gratitude have increasingly been associated with healthier hearts.

Earlier Research Linked Optimism to Healthier Hearts

The new work builds on a prior study led by Hernandez, which found that people with the highest levels of optimism tended to have healthier hearts. That research was published in the journal Health Behavior and Policy Review.

That earlier study was funded by the National Institutes of Health and the National Center for Research Resources. It was co-written with preventive medicine professors Kiarri N. Kershaw, Juned Siddique and Hongyan Ning, all of Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine; preventive medicine and epidemiology professor Donald M. Lloyd-Jones of Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine; psychology professor Julia K. Boehm of Chapman University; social and behavioral sciences professor Laura D. Kubzansky of Harvard University School of Public Health; and Distinguished Professor of Epidemiology Dr. Ana Diez Roux of Drexel University.

articles.personality_title_es: La atención plena y el pensamiento positivo pueden bajar la presión arterial en pocas semanas
articles.personality_presentation_es:

articles.title: Scientists find a human-only gene that may help explain our brainpower
articles.summary: Scientists discovered that human microglia, immune cells that help shape developing brain circuits, can take four to eight years to mature instead of just weeks as they do in mice. The unusually slow process may help explain how the human brain develops its remarkable complexity and cognitive abilities.
articles.content:
Microglia are the brain's most abundant immune cells. They help protect the brain from harmful invaders, clear away damaged neurons, and support normal brain development. Researchers at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute have now found for the first time that human microglia, much like human neurons, mature far more slowly than comparable cells in other animals.

"This slow development may help human microglia influence the human brain in ways that enable our powerful cognitive abilities," said Carlos Diaz-Salazar, PhD, the lead author of a new Neuron study on the subject, who carried out the work while in the lab of Franck Polleux, PhD.

A Human-Specific Gene With an Unusual Role

The Polleux lab has spent more than 15 years studying SRGAP2, one of several dozen genes that were duplicated specifically in humans. The group's broader goal is to understand the biological features that distinguish the human brain from those of other animals.

Earlier work by Dr. Polleux showed that human-specific copies of SRGAP2 increase the number of synapses, or connections, made by neurons while also causing those synapses to mature very slowly. Both traits are distinctive features of human neurons among mammals. The result is a denser and stronger network of neuronal connections that may enhance the brain's ability to process and store information.

In the new research, Dr. Diaz-Salazar found something unexpected. Human-specific copies of SRGAP2 were nearly 10 times more abundant in microglia than in neurons.

"So the question was, 'Why on Earth is this gene so active in microglia?'" recalled Dr. Polleux, a principal investigator at the Zuckerman Institute.

Microglia Help Shape Developing Brain Circuits

Over roughly the past two decades, scientists have learned that microglia do much more than fight infections and help repair brain damage. These cells, which account for 5 to 10 percent of brain cells, also help organize the developing brain.

During development, microglia influence which synapses neurons retain and which ones are eliminated. They can also make synapses more or less responsive, helping fine-tune communication within brain circuits.

Experiments using mice and human cells showed that the human-specific copies of SRGAP2 dramatically slow the development of human microglia. Human microglia take about four to eight years to mature, while microglia in mice reach maturity in roughly three weeks.

"This gene helps control the developmental tempo of neurons, and nature has also selected it to control the development of microglia that are so crucial to neuron development, so they are in sync during development," said Dr. Diaz-Salazar, who is now a researcher at the Hospital del Mar Medical Research Institute in Barcelona.

Why the Human Brain Takes So Long To Mature

Compared with the brains of other mammals, the human brain develops over an unusually long period. Scientists refer to this extended developmental timetable as neoteny, and it is thought to play an important role in the emergence of advanced human cognitive abilities.

The new findings suggest that SRGAP2 may help coordinate this slow developmental pace across multiple kinds of brain cells, including neurons and microglia. The researchers now want to determine exactly how the gene promotes neoteny in these cells and in other parts of the brain.

"We want to understand all the elements that help make up the human brain to understand what makes us unique from an evolutionary standpoint," Dr. Polleux said. "Because scientists have recently found that microglia are involved in neurodevelopmental disorders and neurodegenerative diseases, our findings get us a step closer to understanding what makes human microglia special in the context of brain diseases."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery about a human-specific gene that influences the slow maturation of brain immune cells, which may explain the unique complexity of the human brain and cognitive abilities. This breakthrough has broad implications for understanding human brain development and potential links to neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases, thus offering meaningful benefits to health science and society.

articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren un gen humano que ralentiza el crecimiento de células inmunes cerebrales, explicando nuestro cerebro complejo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han estado investigando por qué el cerebro humano se desarrolla más lentamente y es más complejo que el de otros animales. Una parte importante del cerebro son las microglías, células inmunes que protegen el cerebro y ayudan a su desarrollo.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Columbia descubrieron que las microglías humanas tardan entre cuatro y ocho años en madurar, mucho más que las pocas semanas que tardan en los ratones. Encontraron que un gen llamado SRGAP2, específico de los humanos, está muy activo en estas microglías y ralentiza su desarrollo.

**Impacto** – Este crecimiento lento de las microglías podría explicar cómo el cerebro humano construye conexiones fuertes y complejas durante muchos años. El gen SRGAP2 ya se conocía por ralentizar el desarrollo de las neuronas y aumentar las conexiones cerebrales, pero ahora los científicos ven que también controla las microglías, que apoyan el desarrollo neuronal. Este descubrimiento ayuda a entender por qué el cerebro humano se desarrolla lentamente y adquiere habilidades avanzadas de pensamiento.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores planean estudiar exactamente cómo SRGAP2 controla el desarrollo lento en las células cerebrales y cómo esto podría afectar enfermedades cerebrales como el autismo o el Alzheimer. Entender mejor este gen podría llevar a nuevas formas de tratar o prevenir estas condiciones.

**Una frase clave** – Un gen específico humano llamado SRGAP2 ralentiza el crecimiento de células inmunes cerebrales, ayudando a explicar el largo desarrollo y las habilidades únicas del cerebro humano.

articles.title: How Ukraine created world-leading prostheses amid the chaos of war
articles.summary: Injuries from the war in Ukraine have forced the country to develop highly advanced prostheses and fit them in record numbers. What can the rest of the world learn from its efforts?
articles.content:
Injuries from the war in Ukraine have forced the country to develop highly advanced prostheses and fit them in record numbers. What can the rest of the world learn from its efforts?

A robotic hand created by prosthetics company Esper has advanced capabilities Esper

In the early 1980s, military forces from the Soviet Union went to war in Afghanistan in an effort to prop up a failing Marxist regime. At the time, Ukraine was part of the union, and many of its people were conscripted. Plenty of soldiers ended up losing legs in the fighting – and back then, their options weren’t good.

Shockingly, the Soviet authorities’ response was to offer them a medical version of a skateboard to get around. “That was your only option,” says Antonina Kumka, a former adviser to Ukraine’s government. “They were just rolling on wooden boards with wheels around the cities.”

Fast-forward to today, and Ukrainians have again been thrust into a war they didn’t choose. This time, the conditions of modern warfare mean that unprecedented numbers of people are losing limbs, presenting the country with a huge challenge. The response, however, has been very different. Kumka, who is a co-founder of Protez Hub, an initiative to improve the lot of Ukrainians with amputations, has been stepping up her work. And her organisation is just one part of a sprawling network of clinics, start-ups and research labs that has sprung up to help the injured.

Advertisement

Thankfully, no skateboards are involved. But questions abound. Does Ukraine really have what it needs to help the legions of injured people – many of whom will need prostheses for decades to come? Is this newly created industry always acting in the best interests of those it assists? And it is worth asking what the rest of the world can learn from Ukraine’s booming prosthetics industry.

Unsurprisingly, statistics on the number of Ukrainian amputations are murky. Figures of up to 100,000 are often mentioned in news reports, apparently based on government estimates. But Ukraine has an interest in exaggerating this number to bolster international empathy and support. Kumka, who can access official statistics as part of her work, tells New Scientist the real number is around 24,100, counting from the beginning of 2021 to the end of 2025. (Neither the Ukrainian Ministry of Health nor the Ministry of Social Policy responded to requests to confirm this number.)

However, even that lower estimate represents a tragic loss for a whole generation of Ukrainians. For context, 12,000 UK service members lost limbs in the six years of the second world war, while around 1705 US service members had limbs amputated as a result of injuries sustained during 16 years of fighting in Iraq and Afghanistan. For Ukraine, which had one of the lowest incomes of any European country even before Russia’s invasion, the necessary medical response is an enormous challenge.

Prosthetics have come a long way since the years leading up to the second world war. Here, artificial legs are manufactured in 1930s London Daily Herald Archive/National Science & Media Museum/SSPL via Getty Images

The nature of the war today means that not only are amputations more common – on both sides – but they also tend to be particularly difficult cases. The front lines are shrouded in a wide no-man’s-land, known locally as the Kill Zone, in which drones dominate and no vehicle can move without attracting deadly attention. Anyone from Ukraine injured in this zone faces a difficult extraction that is only partially being addressed with ground drones at the moment.

Yakov Gradinar works at Protez Foundation (which translates as Prosthetics Foundation), a non-profit clinic in Ukraine that supplies and fits prostheses (and which isn’t connected to Protez Hub). He says one person recently came in having been stuck on the front line wearing a tourniquet for 60 days. These devices stem blood loss in the short term, but create complications in the long term. They were simply never designed to be used for such lengthy periods. “Tourniquets are saving lives, but losing limbs,” says Gradinar. He estimates that as many as 95 per cent of these patients would be dead without the life-saving devices, but that they also lead to amputations much higher up the limb because the flesh below them rots once it is deprived of blood flow.

Payments for prosthetics

One of the reasons the prosthetics industry in Ukraine now extends far beyond Gradinar’s organisation comes down to money. Before Russia’s invasion in 2014, Ukraine had only a small number of prosthetics workshops dealing with cases from car accidents and medical amputations. The government would pay almost $700 per limb, which the individual could use as they saw fit. Since then, Kumka has been a leading figure in campaigning for greater investment and better legislation. Now, the Ukrainian government will pay $100,000 to soldiers for each lost limb, allowing them to go to any of the country’s increasingly numerous private clinics, or even abroad, and choose a limb that suits their needs. When limbs wear out after two to five years, they can receive the payment again. (It is a similar situation for civilians who lose a limb, albeit with less money available.) Over the coming years, this will cost the government “billions and billions and billions of dollars”, says Kumka.

This investment has catalysed the development of new clinics, labs and more. Former doctor Dima Gazda launched a company called Esper six years ago – before the full-scale invasion – to develop sensor technology that could be licensed to other companies for use with prostheses. But when the war ratcheted up, Gazda wondered whether this technology could be adapted so the company could create its own prosthesis for wounded soldiers. “The Ukrainian prosthetics market is definitely shaped by war. We as a company, also, we are shaped by war,” he says.

Since then, Esper has developed an advanced robotic prosthetic hand that has six motors controlled by sensors, allowing the wearer to move the hand faster or slower as needed. It is more dextrous and capable than most prosthetic hands. Around 60 per cent of its nearly 250 components are made in Ukraine. The Esper Hand is waterproof, can carry loads of up to 35 kilograms and is highly modular, so breakages can be easily repaired without having to ship it to a service centre. It is also 10 per cent lighter than a human hand – although Gazda says everyone who holds it thinks it is heavy, largely because they have never held a human hand in the same way.

Esper now employs 65 staff, and although its head office is in New York, most of them work in Ukraine. More than 600 soldiers have been fitted with at least one Esper Hand, and more than 50 of those are back on the front line. According to Gadza, one soldier called Volodymr, who lost both arms in a drone attack, has now been fitted with a pair of Esper Hands. He subsequently qualified on an elite sniper course, which he put down to the hands no longer having a pulse running through them, allowing him to be unnaturally still and precise. He also started to paint, and has held his first exhibition.

Since being fitted with two Esper Hands, Ukrainian soldier Volodymyr has taken up a new hobby Esper

Another example of Ukraine’s burgeoning prosthetics industry is Gradinar’s Protez Foundation. Amputations higher up a limb generally lead to a harder rehab, and any prostheses with a knee, which are more difficult to learn to use, are more complex to build and fit, and therefore more expensive. We have long known that higher amputations also result in greater energy use when walking. Not only is Ukraine seeing huge demand for prosthetics care, but it is also seeing the most challenging cases imaginable.

Gradinar says that many new clinics take only the easier cases, but he prides himself on never saying no. He has fitted devices from Icelandic company Össur, which uses resin and glass fibre to mould a socket that fits the user closely, on shorter amputations than the company had ever previously seen done – pushing the boundaries of what was believed to be possible.

Other Ukrainian companies are emerging all the time. Kyiv-based Allbionics makes an electronic hand with 3D-printed construction, backed up by aluminium where needed, which runs for two days on a single charge. A smartphone app helps users learn to operate the device and track usage stats. Syla makes a prosthetic knee that uses AI to help the wearer control it intuitively and lets them walk at up to 10 kilometres an hour, with a battery life of 24 hours. There are also treatment clinics, such as Superhumans Center, which has three sites across Ukraine and more than 600 staff.



A military veteran exercises at a Superhumans rehabilitation centre in the city of Lviv, one of many clinics that have opened to support Ukrainians who have lost limbs Mykhaylo Palinchak

However, it isn’t a uniformly positive picture. Kumka says some prosthetics clinics are spending a great deal on marketing and PR, and are prioritising their bottom line and patient numbers over quality of care. “Prosthetics and amputations in general are very lucrative for charities right now, I’ll be honest,” she says. Patients face multiple pitfalls, she reckons, including clinics that fraudulently fit cheaper devices while claiming the cost of more expensive ones, or charities that seek foreign aid but also apply for government reimbursement for treatment. Gradinar concedes there are problems in places. “It’s corruption, but it’s survival mode,” he says. “It’s getting, each day, better and better.”

The economics of medical devices in wartime can also be jarring. For instance, many prostheses currently fitted in Ukraine come from German company Ottobock. But it also openly sells to Russia. The company told New Scientist that Russia represented 8.8 per cent of its global revenue in the first half of 2025, up from 5 per cent in 2023. A report from a US analytics firm puts the figure at closer to 35 per cent, and says that despite claiming to sell only to civilians, Ottobock’s devices have been seen in footage of Russian soldiers. Ottobock refuted that figure and told New Scientist it doesn’t work directly with the Russian military, but cannot rule out that its devices may end up on its front lines.

On top of that, there’s a more direct worry: that the swift innovation going on in Ukraine may result in Ukrainians being fitted with untested devices in a manner that would be considered unethical in peacetime. “There are so many different companies going into Ukraine with their less-than-perfect solutions and trying to use Ukrainians as [experimental] material,” says Kumka. “They would never pass ethical board regulations [in other countries], and they would never be approved, but in Ukraine, they can do that because nobody stops them. They’re using it as a testing ground.”

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Editor’s Highlights Sign up to newsletter

Finally, despite the number of start-ups and new clinics working on advanced devices, many prosthetics experts believe there remains a critical shortage: medical expertise. On average, someone with an amputation requires nine medical visits in the first year alone, whether that be fittings, physiotherapy appointments or psychological support. And even when the prosthesis is in place, that isn’t the end. Amputation surgery causes a great deal of swelling, so the person being treated often finds that their first prosthesis quickly becomes ill-fitting as the limb heals and reduces in size. Given all of this, prosthetics engineer Alex Dickinson at the University of Southampton, UK, says the biggest problem in Ukraine isn’t necessarily to do with the prosthetics hardware. “It’s the [lack of] trained clinicians,” he says.

In the medium term, there will be further changes, as muscles that once had a strenuous job find themselves doing much less, or even nothing at all, and atrophy, while others get stronger. So, someone may have three prosthetic limbs in their first year.

Then, in the longer term, prostheses simply wear out. Once an individual has adapted, this can happen every two to five years, meaning they may get through a dozen or more in their lifetime. “It’s a really good sign [when a prosthetic] leg falls apart, because it shows the person’s working really hard on it. It actually got them back to really good physical activity,” says Dickinson. “So, it’s lifetime care that these people need.”

Ukraine has already shown itself capable of building a drone industry from scratch, reducing its reliance on politically problematic supply chains, then becoming a global expert and exporting its knowledge and products around Europe and the US. It is possible the same could happen with prostheses – the fact that Esper now has a head office in the US may be a sign of that.

Still, it is fair to say that helping people with amputations adapt to their new lived reality goes far beyond fitting a prosthesis or even providing ongoing mental health support. Take the fact that cities in Ukraine aren’t exactly known for their ease of access for people with disabilities. On a recent reporting trip to Kyiv, I was struck by the city’s beauty, but surprised by how car-centric and hostile to pedestrians parts of it were.

Many of those who have lost limbs are young men with long lives ahead of them, which perhaps explains why there is now plenty of talk about addressing this problem. The military veteran and double amputee Oleksandr Budko has a YouTube show in which he takes Ukrainian celebrities to different cities to test them for accessibility. In one episode, he and television presenter Masha Efrosynina roll through Lviv in wheelchairs, growing increasingly frustrated by the cobbled streets and their inability to get up the steps into cafes.

Making old cities accessible is vital in every country, but for Ukraine, the need is being thrust into the mainstream by a young generation of recently injured people. As the country rebuilds in the coming years, it will need to ensure that it is done with accessibility first and foremost in mind – and Budko has found that city governments contact him after his shows air for advice. All this will take time, no doubt, but we have already come a long way from those medical skateboards.

These devices help people regain movement and even take on new skills, like a soldier who became an elite sniper and artist after being fitted with prosthetic hands.
